# Alfred North Whitehead Summary
Alfred North Whitehead was an English mathematician and philosopher born in Ramsgate, Kent, in 1861. He studied mathematics at Trinity College, Cambridge, where he earned his B.A. in 1884. Whitehead taught and wrote on mathematics and physics at Cambridge until 1910, during which time he collaborated with Bertrand Russell on the first edition of *Principia Mathematica* . Later, in 1914, he became a professor of applied mathematics at Imperial College London, before taking up a position at Harvard University in 1924.
He is recognized for significant contributions to metaphysics and philosophy, developing a "process" ontology which rejects the Cartesian idea of fundamentally independent matter in favor of an event-based reality where all entities are interrelated. His philosophy, often termed "process philosophy," views reality as composed of discrete "occasions of experience" and emphasizes that relations take a primary role. Whitehead's thought on religion suggests a conception of God that is not a divine king, but rather operates through quiet love and is changed by the world's activity. Furthermore, he was a deep proponent of educational reform, cautioning against teaching "inert ideas" and advocating for education to be transdisciplinary and value-laden.
